nameStory: The 'belted' whiteface gets its name from the distinctive reddish band that wraps around its waist like a tiny belt. The 'whiteface' part comes from the bright white patch on the front of its head, which looks almost like it's wearing face paint. This snowy-white facial marking is the signature feature that all whiteface dragonflies share.
description: The Belted Whiteface is a medium-sized dragonfly that's part of the skimmer family, known for their habit of perching on vegetation and 'skimming' over water surfaces. This striking insect has a dark body accented by a bright reddish belt around its middle section and the characteristic white face that gives it its name. Adults typically measure about 1.5 inches in length with a wingspan of roughly 2.5 inches. You'll often see them perched on emergent plants near ponds and wetlands, where they hunt smaller flying insects.

idTips.label: White face patch
idTips.description: Look for the bright white coloring on the front of the head (the frons) that contrasts sharply with the dark body - it's so white it almost glows in sunlight

idTips.label: Reddish belt marking
idTips.description: A distinctive red to orange band wraps around the middle segments of the abdomen, clearly visible when the dragonfly is perched

idTips.label: Dark body coloration
idTips.description: The overall body appears black or very dark brown, creating strong contrast with the white face and red belt

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often seen sitting motionless on reed tips or other vertical stems emerging from water, returning to the same perch repeatedly

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are transparent with dark veining and may show a slight amber tinge at the base, held perpendicular to the body when at rest

habitat: Belted Whitefaces prefer acidic wetlands including bogs, fens, and marshy ponds surrounded by sphagnum moss and sedges. In New England, look for them around mountain ponds, beaver wetlands, and northern bogs where they perch on emergent vegetation like cattails and rushes. They're more common in northern areas and higher elevations where cooler, acidic conditions prevail.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, usually May in southern New England. Fresh individuals may appear pale and soft-bodied as their exoskeletons harden.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from June through August when adults are actively hunting, mating, and laying eggs. This is the best time for identification as colors are most vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly by September, though some individuals may persist into early fall during warm weather before dying off with the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they overwinter as aquatic nymphs (larvae) in pond sediments, developing slowly in the cold water until ready to emerge the following year.

funFact: Belted Whitefaces are essentially flying fighter jets - they can see in nearly 360 degrees thanks to compound eyes containing up to 30,000 individual lenses, and they catch about 95% of the prey they target, making them more successful hunters than lions or sharks!
confusionNotes: The white face immediately separates this from most other dragonflies, but it can be confused with other whiteface species. The key memory trick: 'Belted has the belt' - that reddish band around the middle is unique among New England whitefaces and is your best field mark when combined with the white face.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'whiteface' can be confusing because it refers to the technical term 'frons' - the front part of an insect's head between the eyes. Many people initially look for a completely white head, but it's just this front facial area that's white while the rest of the head remains dark.
compareHints: Among New England's whitefaces, the Belted is the only one with that distinctive red belt around its waist - other whitefaces like the Dot-tailed have spots or different markings but lack this wraparound band. The Hudsonian Whiteface is similar in size but has yellow markings instead of red, while the smaller Dot-tailed has a distinctive white-tipped tail rather than a belted middle.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's whitefaces, the dot-tailed whiteface is distinguished by its spotted abdomen pattern.
Compared to its whiteface relatives, the frosted whiteface is distinguished by the mature male's chalky, pruinose coating that's more extensive than in other species.
Among the whitefaces, Hudsonian Whitefaces are distinguished mainly by habitat preference rather than dramatic physical differences.

Among New England's whitefaces, the Crimson-ringed is distinguished by its bold red abdominal rings, while the Dot-tailed has yellow spots, the Frosted appears more powdery white, and the Hudsonian has more subdued markings.
